{{Short description|Complex analysis function}}
{{More footnotes|date=March 2021}}
In [[mathematics]], in the field of [[complex analysis]], a '''Nevanlinna function'''  is a [[complex function]] which is an [[analytic function]] on the open [[upper half-plane]] <math>\, \mathcal{H} \,</math> and has a non-negative [[imaginary part]]. A Nevanlinna function maps the upper half-plane to itself or a real constant,<ref>A real number is not considered to be in the upper half-plane.</ref> but is [[necessity and sufficiency|not necessarily]] [[injective]] or [[surjective]]. Functions with this property are sometimes also known as '''Herglotz''', '''Pick''' or '''R''' functions.

==Integral representation==

Every Nevanlinna function {{mvar|N}} admits a representation

:<math> N(z) = C + D z + \int_{\mathbb{R}} \bigg(\frac{1}{\lambda - z} - \frac{\lambda}{1 + \lambda^2} \bigg) \operatorname{d} \mu(\lambda), \quad z \in \mathcal{H},</math>

where {{mvar|C}} is a real constant, {{mvar|D}} is a non-negative constant, <math>\mathcal{H}</math> is the [[upper half-plane]], and {{mvar|μ}} is a [[Borel measure]] on [[real numbers|{{math|ℝ}}]] satisfying the growth condition
 
:<math> \int_{\mathbb{R}} \frac{\operatorname{d} \mu(\lambda)}{1 + \lambda^2} < \infty.</math>

Conversely, every function of this form turns out to be a Nevanlinna function. 
The constants in this representation are related to the function {{mvar|N}} via

:<math>  C = \Re \big( N(i) \big) \qquad \text{ and } \qquad D = \lim_{y \rightarrow \infty} \frac{N(i y)}{i y} </math>

and the [[Borel measure]] {{mvar|μ}} can be recovered from {{mvar|N}} by employing the [[Stieltjes inversion formula]] (related to the inversion formula for the [[Stieltjes transformation]]):

:<math> \mu \big( (\lambda_1, \lambda_2 ] \big) = 
\lim_{\delta\rightarrow 0} \lim_{\varepsilon\rightarrow 0} 
\frac{1}{\pi} \int_{\lambda_1+\delta}^{\lambda_2+\delta} \Im \big( N(\lambda + i \varepsilon) \big) \operatorname{d} \lambda.</math>

A very similar representation of functions is also called the [[Poisson representation]].<ref>See for example Section&nbsp;4, "Poisson representation" in {{cite book |title=Hilbert Spaces of Entire Functions |publisher=Prentice-Hall |author=[[Louis de Branges]] |date=1968 |asin=B0006BUXNM}} De Branges gives a form for functions whose '''''real''''' part is non-negative in the upper half-plane.</ref>

==Examples==
Some elementary examples of Nevanlinna functions follow (with appropriately chosen [[Branch point#Branch cuts|branch cuts]] in the first three). (<math>z</math> can be replaced by <math>z - a</math> for any real number <math>a</math>.)

*<math>z^p\text{ with } 0 \le p \le 1</math>

*<math>-z^p\text{ with } -1 \le p \le 0</math>

:::These are [[injective]] but when {{mvar|p}} does not equal 1 or −1 they are not [[surjective]] and can be rotated to some extent around the origin, such as <math>i(z/i)^p ~\text{ with }~-1\le p\le 1</math>.

*A sheet of <math>\ln(z)</math> such as the one with <math>f(1)=0</math>.

*<math>\tan(z)</math> (an example that is surjective but not injective).

* A [[Möbius transformation]]

::<math>z \mapsto  \frac{az+b}{cz+d} </math>

: is a Nevanlinna function if (sufficient but not necessary) <math>\overline{a} d - b \overline{c}</math> is a positive real number and <math>\Im (\overline{b} d ) = \Im (\overline{a} c) = 0</math>. This is equivalent to the set of such transformations that map the real axis to itself. One may then add any constant in the upper half-plane, and move the pole into the lower half-plane, giving new values for the parameters. Example: <math>\frac{i z + i - 2}{z + 1 + i}</math>

* <math>1 + i + z</math> and <math>i + \operatorname{e}^{i z}</math> are examples which are [[entire function]]s. The second is neither injective nor surjective.
* If {{mvar|S}} is a [[self-adjoint operator]] in a [[Hilbert space]] and <math>f</math> is an arbitrary vector, then the function

::<math> \langle (S-z)^{-1} f, f \rangle </math>

: is a Nevanlinna function.

* If <math>M(z)</math> and <math>N(z)</math> are both Nevanlinna functions, then the [[function composition|composition]] <math>M \big( N(z) \big)</math> is a Nevanlinna function as well.

==Importance in operator theory==

Nevanlinna functions appear in the study of [[Operator monotone function]]s.
